question_text: A requirement can appear in three different forms during a project: as a user need, as a system rule, and as a documented form. Using an example of your own choosing, explain the difference between a user need and a system rule, and then state what the documented form contributes that the other two, on their own, cannot.
rubric: 1 mark for correctly characterising the user need as the goal in the user's own language. 1 mark for correctly characterising the system rule as the capability the system must provide to meet it. 1 mark for a valid self-chosen example carried consistently through both forms. 1 mark for identifying a distinct contribution of the documented form (durable record, single shared interpretation, traceability, or something to validate against).
model_answer: A user need is the goal expressed in the user's own language, for example "I want to know whether a book is on the shelf before I walk across campus to fetch it." It states what the person is trying to achieve and says nothing about the system. A system rule is the capability the system must provide to meet that need, for example "The system shall display the availability status of every catalogued title to any logged-in member." It is written for developers and testers, is precise about who and what, and can be tested. The documented form is the written record of either one, such as a user story card or a numbered SRS entry. What it uniquely contributes is persistence and shared reference: a need voiced in a meeting lives only in memory and drifts, whereas the written record communicates one single interpretation to engineer, tester and client alike, preserves it across the project, and allows it to be reviewed, traced back to the stakeholder who asked for it, and traced forward to a design decision and a test case.

question_text: A team building an online examination portal has run out of time and must cut scope two weeks before release. Using the MoSCoW technique, explain the difference between a "Should have" and a "Could have" requirement, and explain why it is still worth formally recording the items the team has agreed NOT to build in this release.
rubric: 1 mark for explaining Should have (important but not vital, a workaround exists). 1 mark for explaining Could have (desirable, adds value, not critical to core function). 1 mark for articulating the boundary between the two rather than placing two definitions side by side, ideally with an exam portal example. 1 mark for one sound, developed reason for recording Won't haves.
model_answer: A Should have is important but not vital for the first release: its absence causes real pain, but the system still functions and the gap can be temporarily worked around. Automatic emailing of results is a Should have for the exam portal, since an administrator can send them manually instead. A Could have is desirable and adds value but is not critical to the core function, and nothing has to be worked around if it is absent, such as a screen showing a student's past attempts. The distinction is therefore the consequence of omission and whether someone must fill the gap by other means, so with two weeks left the team drops Could haves first. Recording the Won't haves is still worthwhile because it turns the exclusion into an agreed, written decision rather than an oversight, it prevents the item being quietly reintroduced during the final fortnight as scope creep, it manages stakeholder expectations honestly by showing that a request was heard and deferred rather than ignored, and it preserves the analysis already done as the starting point for the next release.
student_answer: from the phrase itself we can identify should have requirement sounds it is important and could have requirement sounds more desirable with lowest priority. Both requirements are not neccassary for the system to work.  But the priority for should have requirements are higher than could have requirements.

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Validation asks whether the requirements reflect what stakeholders actually need, which can only be answered against real people and real source documents that the tool cannot access, so an independent human review is essential. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.
student_answer: Danger of allowing the same AI to check its own output.The AI tool will miss its blindspots again and again. Focuses more on the grammatical part over the accuracy of the system. Self checking is not validation it’s just repetition.

question_text: A consultant skipped fact-finding entirely and began interviewing staff at a client's warehouse on day one. Describe two specific outputs that fact-finding would have produced before those interviews began, and explain how agreeing the system's scope at this early stage reduces requirement instability later in the project.
rubric: 1 mark for a first valid fact-finding output identified and given specific warehouse content (half marks if merely named with no context). 1 mark for a second, genuinely distinct output given specific content. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism, that an agreed scope acts as a baseline so later out-of-scope requests are recognised and handled as changes. 1 mark for linking this explicitly to reduced requirement instability, less rework, or less scope creep.
model_answer: The first output is a defined system scope with boundaries and external interfaces: an agreed statement that goods receipt, put-away, picking and stock levels are included, that payroll and rostering for warehouse staff are excluded, and that an interface to the existing accounting package is required. Without it every request a storeman raises sounds equally in scope. The second is an overview of the existing processes together with an identified stakeholder list across all levels, mapping how goods currently move through the warehouse and naming the floor staff, the stock controller, the dispatch supervisor, the finance team who consume the stock figures and the IT staff who will maintain the system, since otherwise the consultant cannot know whom to interview and will forget exactly those groups. Agreeing scope reduces later instability because the boundary becomes a baseline: every requirement collected afterwards can be tested against it, so a request falling outside is recognised as a change to be costed and approved rather than absorbed silently as scope creep. It also forces disagreements to surface in week one for the price of a meeting rather than in month five for the price of a redesign, and because the exclusions are explicit it removes the largest source of late argument, which is the assumption that the system would obviously cover something.

rubric: 1 mark for explaining Should have (important but not vital, a workaround exists). 1 mark for explaining Could have (desirable, adds value, not critical to core function). 1 mark for articulating the boundary between the two rather than placing two definitions side by side, ideally with an exam portal example. 1 mark for one sound, developed reason for recording Won't haves.
model_answer: A Should have is important but not vital for the first release: its absence causes real pain, but the system still functions and the gap can be temporarily worked around. Automatic emailing of results is a Should have for the exam portal, since an administrator can send them manually instead. A Could have is desirable and adds value but is not critical to the core function, and nothing has to be worked around if it is absent, such as a screen showing a student's past attempts. The distinction is therefore the consequence of omission and whether someone must fill the gap by other means, so with two weeks left the team drops Could haves first. Recording the Won't haves is still worthwhile because it turns the exclusion into an agreed, written decision rather than an oversight, it prevents the item being quietly reintroduced during the final fortnight as scope creep, it manages stakeholder expectations honestly by showing that a request was heard and deferred rather than ignored, and it preserves the analysis already done as the starting point for the next release.

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Validation asks whether the requirements reflect what stakeholders actually need, which can only be answered against real people and real source documents that the tool cannot access, so an independent human review is essential. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.

question_text: A consultant skipped fact-finding entirely and began interviewing staff at a client's warehouse on day one. Describe two specific outputs that fact-finding would have produced before those interviews began, and explain how agreeing the system's scope at this early stage reduces requirement instability later in the project.
rubric: 1 mark for a first valid fact-finding output identified and given specific warehouse content (half marks if merely named with no context). 1 mark for a second, genuinely distinct output given specific content. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism, that an agreed scope acts as a baseline so later out-of-scope requests are recognised and handled as changes. 1 mark for linking this explicitly to reduced requirement instability, less rework, or less scope creep.
model_answer: The first output is a defined system scope with boundaries and external interfaces: an agreed statement that goods receipt, put-away, picking and stock levels are included, that payroll and rostering for warehouse staff are excluded, and that an interface to the existing accounting package is required. Without it every request a storeman raises sounds equally in scope. The second is an overview of the existing processes together with an identified stakeholder list across all levels, mapping how goods currently move through the warehouse and naming the floor staff, the stock controller, the dispatch supervisor, the finance team who consume the stock figures and the IT staff who will maintain the system, since otherwise the consultant cannot know whom to interview and will forget exactly those groups. Agreeing scope reduces later instability because the boundary becomes a baseline: every requirement collected afterwards can be tested against it, so a request falling outside is recognised as a change to be costed and approved rather than absorbed silently as scope creep. It also forces disagreements to surface in week one for the price of a meeting rather than in month five for the price of a redesign, and because the exclusions are explicit it removes the largest source of late argument, which is the assumption that the system would obviously cover something.

question_text: A requirement can appear in three different forms during a project: as a user need, as a system rule, and as a documented form. Using an example of your own choosing, explain the difference between a user need and a system rule, and then state what the documented form contributes that the other two, on their own, cannot.
rubric: 1 mark for correctly characterising the user need as the goal in the user's own language. 1 mark for correctly characterising the system rule as the capability the system must provide to meet it. 1 mark for a valid self-chosen example carried consistently through both forms. 1 mark for identifying a distinct contribution of the documented form (durable record, single shared interpretation, traceability, or something to validate against).
model_answer: A user need is the goal expressed in the user's own language, for example "I want to know whether a book is on the shelf before I walk across campus to fetch it." It states what the person is trying to achieve and says nothing about the system. A system rule is the capability the system must provide to meet that need, for example "The system shall display the availability status of every catalogued title to any logged-in member." It is written for developers and testers, is precise about who and what, and can be tested. The documented form is the written record of either one, such as a user story card or a numbered SRS entry. What it uniquely contributes is persistence and shared reference: a need voiced in a meeting lives only in memory and drifts, whereas the written record communicates one single interpretation to engineer, tester and client alike, preserves it across the project, and allows it to be reviewed, traced back to the stakeholder who asked for it, and traced forward to a design decision and a test case.

rubric: 1 mark for a first valid fact-finding output identified and given specific warehouse content (half marks if merely named with no context). 1 mark for a second, genuinely distinct output given specific content. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism, that an agreed scope acts as a baseline so later out-of-scope requests are recognised and handled as changes. 1 mark for linking this explicitly to reduced requirement instability, less rework, or less scope creep.
model_answer: The first output is a defined system scope with boundaries and external interfaces: an agreed statement that goods receipt, put-away, picking and stock levels are included, that payroll and rostering for warehouse staff are excluded, and that an interface to the existing accounting package is required. Without it every request a storeman raises sounds equally in scope. The second is an overview of the existing processes together with an identified stakeholder list across all levels, mapping how goods currently move through the warehouse and naming the floor staff, the stock controller, the dispatch supervisor, the finance team who consume the stock figures and the IT staff who will maintain the system, since otherwise the consultant cannot know whom to interview and will forget exactly those groups. Agreeing scope reduces later instability because the boundary becomes a baseline: every requirement collected afterwards can be tested against it, so a request falling outside is recognised as a change to be costed and approved rather than absorbed silently as scope creep. It also forces disagreements to surface in week one for the price of a meeting rather than in month five for the price of a redesign, and because the exclusions are explicit it removes the largest source of late argument, which is the assumption that the system would obviously cover something.
student_answer: Output -   How the work/process at the warehouse is actually going on, in a daily basis.   The consultant would have a better understanding about what the staff wants, when interviewing them.      This reduces requirement instability later in the project, because the development team will have a better understanding about user requirements and wont have to rebuild the functions of the system, which will save time, money and effort of the entire system.

question_text: A requirement can appear in three different forms during a project: as a user need, as a system rule, and as a documented form. Using an example of your own choosing, explain the difference between a user need and a system rule, and then state what the documented form contributes that the other two, on their own, cannot.
rubric: 1 mark for correctly characterising the user need as the goal in the user's own language. 1 mark for correctly characterising the system rule as the capability the system must provide to meet it. 1 mark for a valid self-chosen example carried consistently through both forms. 1 mark for identifying a distinct contribution of the documented form (durable record, single shared interpretation, traceability, or something to validate against).
model_answer: A user need is the goal expressed in the user's own language, for example "I want to know whether a book is on the shelf before I walk across campus to fetch it." It states what the person is trying to achieve and says nothing about the system. A system rule is the capability the system must provide to meet that need, for example "The system shall display the availability status of every catalogued title to any logged-in member." It is written for developers and testers, is precise about who and what, and can be tested. The documented form is the written record of either one, such as a user story card or a numbered SRS entry. What it uniquely contributes is persistence and shared reference: a need voiced in a meeting lives only in memory and drifts, whereas the written record communicates one single interpretation to engineer, tester and client alike, preserves it across the project, and allows it to be reviewed, traced back to the stakeholder who asked for it, and traced forward to a design decision and a test case.

Documented form shows the regulation and the laws that were used to obtain data from that third party user asked to get data from and then show what kind of implementing process that was done by the developing team.

question_text: A team building an online examination portal has run out of time and must cut scope two weeks before release. Using the MoSCoW technique, explain the difference between a "Should have" and a "Could have" requirement, and explain why it is still worth formally recording the items the team has agreed NOT to build in this release.
rubric: 1 mark for explaining Should have (important but not vital, a workaround exists). 1 mark for explaining Could have (desirable, adds value, not critical to core function). 1 mark for articulating the boundary between the two rather than placing two definitions side by side, ideally with an exam portal example. 1 mark for one sound, developed reason for recording Won't haves.
model_answer: A Should have is important but not vital for the first release: its absence causes real pain, but the system still functions and the gap can be temporarily worked around. Automatic emailing of results is a Should have for the exam portal, since an administrator can send them manually instead. A Could have is desirable and adds value but is not critical to the core function, and nothing has to be worked around if it is absent, such as a screen showing a student's past attempts. The distinction is therefore the consequence of omission and whether someone must fill the gap by other means, so with two weeks left the team drops Could haves first. Recording the Won't haves is still worthwhile because it turns the exclusion into an agreed, written decision rather than an oversight, it prevents the item being quietly reintroduced during the final fortnight as scope creep, it manages stakeholder expectations honestly by showing that a request was heard and deferred rather than ignored, and it preserves the analysis already done as the starting point for the next release.
student_answer: Should have - It should have the basic functions that needs to design the online examination.   (Should be able to enter student records and keep them / Should be able to enter student identification and face an online exam / should be able get results etc.)      Could have - These are the things that makes the online examination portal attractive and suer friendly in a best way.   (Could have an popup msg system saying that there is an exam due to do, could have an attractive and dynamic styled form to fill student records)      why it is still worth formally recording the items the team has agreed not to build?   It will be useful to keep that listed, so in the future, maybe in the maintenance process, we could upgrade the system with them and make the website more user friendly.

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Validation asks whether the requirements reflect what stakeholders actually need, which can only be answered against real people and real source documents that the tool cannot access, so an independent human review is essential. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.
student_answer: The whole system that you produced are going to be stored in ai tools databases. So when another ai user asks similar requirement from the ai tools, there is a chance that the ai tools will give your code snippets to that user. So, this will violate the commercial rights of that site/system you made for that particular user. If there are data that are highly confidential, the developing team will face legal issues.   The person who carries the professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail is the project manager who overlooks the project.

question_text: A team building an online examination portal has run out of time and must cut scope two weeks before release. Using the MoSCoW technique, explain the difference between a "Should have" and a "Could have" requirement, and explain why it is still worth formally recording the items the team has agreed NOT to build in this release.
rubric: 1 mark for explaining Should have (important but not vital, a workaround exists). 1 mark for explaining Could have (desirable, adds value, not critical to core function). 1 mark for articulating the boundary between the two rather than placing two definitions side by side, ideally with an exam portal example. 1 mark for one sound, developed reason for recording Won't haves.
model_answer: A Should have is important but not vital for the first release: its absence causes real pain, but the system still functions and the gap can be temporarily worked around. Automatic emailing of results is a Should have for the exam portal, since an administrator can send them manually instead. A Could have is desirable and adds value but is not critical to the core function, and nothing has to be worked around if it is absent, such as a screen showing a student's past attempts. The distinction is therefore the consequence of omission and whether someone must fill the gap by other means, so with two weeks left the team drops Could haves first. Recording the Won't haves is still worthwhile because it turns the exclusion into an agreed, written decision rather than an oversight, it prevents the item being quietly reintroduced during the final fortnight as scope creep, it manages stakeholder expectations honestly by showing that a request was heard and deferred rather than ignored, and it preserves the analysis already done as the starting point for the next release.

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Validation asks whether the requirements reflect what stakeholders actually need, which can only be answered against real people and real source documents that the tool cannot access, so an independent human review is essential. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.

This will lead to inaccurate or misleading requirements when the system is being built.      The requirements engineer carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes issues.

question_text: A consultant skipped fact-finding entirely and began interviewing staff at a client's warehouse on day one. Describe two specific outputs that fact-finding would have produced before those interviews began, and explain how agreeing the system's scope at this early stage reduces requirement instability later in the project.
rubric: 1 mark for a first valid fact-finding output identified and given specific warehouse content (half marks if merely named with no context). 1 mark for a second, genuinely distinct output given specific content. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism, that an agreed scope acts as a baseline so later out-of-scope requests are recognised and handled as changes. 1 mark for linking this explicitly to reduced requirement instability, less rework, or less scope creep.
model_answer: The first output is a defined system scope with boundaries and external interfaces: an agreed statement that goods receipt, put-away, picking and stock levels are included, that payroll and rostering for warehouse staff are excluded, and that an interface to the existing accounting package is required. Without it every request a storeman raises sounds equally in scope. The second is an overview of the existing processes together with an identified stakeholder list across all levels, mapping how goods currently move through the warehouse and naming the floor staff, the stock controller, the dispatch supervisor, the finance team who consume the stock figures and the IT staff who will maintain the system, since otherwise the consultant cannot know whom to interview and will forget exactly those groups. Agreeing scope reduces later instability because the boundary becomes a baseline: every requirement collected afterwards can be tested against it, so a request falling outside is recognised as a change to be costed and approved rather than absorbed silently as scope creep. It also forces disagreements to surface in week one for the price of a meeting rather than in month five for the price of a redesign, and because the exclusions are explicit it removes the largest source of late argument, which is the assumption that the system would obviously cover something.

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.

rubric: 1 mark for correctly characterising the user need as the goal in the user's own language. 1 mark for correctly characterising the system rule as the capability the system must provide to meet it. 1 mark for a valid self-chosen example carried consistently through both forms. 1 mark for identifying a distinct contribution of the documented form (durable record, single shared interpretation, traceability, or something to validate against).
model_answer: A user need is the goal expressed in the user's own language, for example "I want to know whether a book is on the shelf before I walk across campus to fetch it." It states what the person is trying to achieve and says nothing about the system. A system rule is the capability the system must provide to meet that need, for example "The system shall display the availability status of every catalogued title to any logged-in member." It is written for developers and testers, is precise about who and what, and can be tested. The documented form is the written record of either one, such as a user story card or a numbered SRS entry. What it uniquely contributes is persistence and shared reference: a need voiced in a meeting lives only in memory and drifts, whereas the written record communicates one single interpretation to engineer, tester and client alike, preserves it across the project, and allows it to be reviewed, traced back to the stakeholder who asked for it, and traced forward to a design decision and a test case.

question_text: A team building an online examination portal has run out of time and must cut scope two weeks before release. Using the MoSCoW technique, explain the difference between a "Should have" and a "Could have" requirement, and explain why it is still worth formally recording the items the team has agreed NOT to build in this release.
rubric: 1 mark for explaining Should have (important but not vital, a workaround exists). 1 mark for explaining Could have (desirable, adds value, not critical to core function). 1 mark for articulating the boundary between the two rather than placing two definitions side by side, ideally with an exam portal example. 1 mark for one sound, developed reason for recording Won't haves.
model_answer: A Should have is important but not vital for the first release: its absence causes real pain, but the system still functions and the gap can be temporarily worked around. Automatic emailing of results is a Should have for the exam portal, since an administrator can send them manually instead. A Could have is desirable and adds value but is not critical to the core function, and nothing has to be worked around if it is absent, such as a screen showing a student's past attempts. The distinction is therefore the consequence of omission and whether someone must fill the gap by other means, so with two weeks left the team drops Could haves first. Recording the Won't haves is still worthwhile because it turns the exclusion into an agreed, written decision rather than an oversight, it prevents the item being quietly reintroduced during the final fortnight as scope creep, it manages stakeholder expectations honestly by showing that a request was heard and deferred rather than ignored, and it preserves the analysis already done as the starting point for the next release.
student_answer: The difference is that should have requirements are important and should be include whenever possible, while could have requirements are optional enhancement with less impact on the system      A should have requirement is important and add significant value, but the system can still be released without it if necessary. for example in an online examination portal, automatic email notifications after submitting an exam are a should have feature      A could have requirement is desirable but has a lower priority and only gets implemented if there is enough time and resources. for example dark mode or custom themes are could have features

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Validation asks whether the requirements reflect what stakeholders actually need, which can only be answered against real people and real source documents that the tool cannot access, so an independent human review is essential. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.
student_answer: using the same AI to write and review requirements may miss its own mistakes      humans must review and approve them   if the system fails the project team/organization is responsible, not the AI

question_text: A consultant skipped fact-finding entirely and began interviewing staff at a client's warehouse on day one. Describe two specific outputs that fact-finding would have produced before those interviews began, and explain how agreeing the system's scope at this early stage reduces requirement instability later in the project.
rubric: 1 mark for a first valid fact-finding output identified and given specific warehouse content (half marks if merely named with no context). 1 mark for a second, genuinely distinct output given specific content. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism, that an agreed scope acts as a baseline so later out-of-scope requests are recognised and handled as changes. 1 mark for linking this explicitly to reduced requirement instability, less rework, or less scope creep.
model_answer: The first output is a defined system scope with boundaries and external interfaces: an agreed statement that goods receipt, put-away, picking and stock levels are included, that payroll and rostering for warehouse staff are excluded, and that an interface to the existing accounting package is required. Without it every request a storeman raises sounds equally in scope. The second is an overview of the existing processes together with an identified stakeholder list across all levels, mapping how goods currently move through the warehouse and naming the floor staff, the stock controller, the dispatch supervisor, the finance team who consume the stock figures and the IT staff who will maintain the system, since otherwise the consultant cannot know whom to interview and will forget exactly those groups. Agreeing scope reduces later instability because the boundary becomes a baseline: every requirement collected afterwards can be tested against it, so a request falling outside is recognised as a change to be costed and approved rather than absorbed silently as scope creep. It also forces disagreements to surface in week one for the price of a meeting rather than in month five for the price of a redesign, and because the exclusions are explicit it removes the largest source of late argument, which is the assumption that the system would obviously cover something.
student_answer: Two outputs of fact-finding are:   system scope/stakeholder requirements   agreeing the scope early prevents scope creep, reduces requirement changes, and keeps the project stable

rubric: 1 mark for explaining Should have (important but not vital, a workaround exists). 1 mark for explaining Could have (desirable, adds value, not critical to core function). 1 mark for articulating the boundary between the two rather than placing two definitions side by side, ideally with an exam portal example. 1 mark for one sound, developed reason for recording Won't haves.
model_answer: A Should have is important but not vital for the first release: its absence causes real pain, but the system still functions and the gap can be temporarily worked around. Automatic emailing of results is a Should have for the exam portal, since an administrator can send them manually instead. A Could have is desirable and adds value but is not critical to the core function, and nothing has to be worked around if it is absent, such as a screen showing a student's past attempts. The distinction is therefore the consequence of omission and whether someone must fill the gap by other means, so with two weeks left the team drops Could haves first. Recording the Won't haves is still worthwhile because it turns the exclusion into an agreed, written decision rather than an oversight, it prevents the item being quietly reintroduced during the final fortnight as scope creep, it manages stakeholder expectations honestly by showing that a request was heard and deferred rather than ignored, and it preserves the analysis already done as the starting point for the next release.
student_answer: "Should have" requirement can also be considered as a functional requirement which explains about the main features the system should contain and "could have" requirement can be classified as non functional requirements which explain the constraints, security, limits and reliability of the system which are nice to have requirements of a system.      By formally recording the items the team has not agreed to build, it is easy to focus on what the team should build and give attention to those

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Validation asks whether the requirements reflect what stakeholders actually need, which can only be answered against real people and real source documents that the tool cannot access, so an independent human review is essential. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.
student_answer: AI models can be overconfident with their response and it can comment positively about the quality of the requirement even though it clearly might be not   If the developed system fails the developer who drafted the requirements will be held responsible

question_text: A consultant skipped fact-finding entirely and began interviewing staff at a client's warehouse on day one. Describe two specific outputs that fact-finding would have produced before those interviews began, and explain how agreeing the system's scope at this early stage reduces requirement instability later in the project.
rubric: 1 mark for a first valid fact-finding output identified and given specific warehouse content (half marks if merely named with no context). 1 mark for a second, genuinely distinct output given specific content. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism, that an agreed scope acts as a baseline so later out-of-scope requests are recognised and handled as changes. 1 mark for linking this explicitly to reduced requirement instability, less rework, or less scope creep.
model_answer: The first output is a defined system scope with boundaries and external interfaces: an agreed statement that goods receipt, put-away, picking and stock levels are included, that payroll and rostering for warehouse staff are excluded, and that an interface to the existing accounting package is required. Without it every request a storeman raises sounds equally in scope. The second is an overview of the existing processes together with an identified stakeholder list across all levels, mapping how goods currently move through the warehouse and naming the floor staff, the stock controller, the dispatch supervisor, the finance team who consume the stock figures and the IT staff who will maintain the system, since otherwise the consultant cannot know whom to interview and will forget exactly those groups. Agreeing scope reduces later instability because the boundary becomes a baseline: every requirement collected afterwards can be tested against it, so a request falling outside is recognised as a change to be costed and approved rather than absorbed silently as scope creep. It also forces disagreements to surface in week one for the price of a meeting rather than in month five for the price of a redesign, and because the exclusions are explicit it removes the largest source of late argument, which is the assumption that the system would obviously cover something.
student_answer: He could have got an idea about how the warehouse operates   He could have identified the processes involved in the warehouse

question_text: A requirement can appear in three different forms during a project: as a user need, as a system rule, and as a documented form. Using an example of your own choosing, explain the difference between a user need and a system rule, and then state what the documented form contributes that the other two, on their own, cannot.
rubric: 1 mark for correctly characterising the user need as the goal in the user's own language. 1 mark for correctly characterising the system rule as the capability the system must provide to meet it. 1 mark for a valid self-chosen example carried consistently through both forms. 1 mark for identifying a distinct contribution of the documented form (durable record, single shared interpretation, traceability, or something to validate against).
model_answer: A user need is the goal expressed in the user's own language, for example "I want to know whether a book is on the shelf before I walk across campus to fetch it." It states what the person is trying to achieve and says nothing about the system. A system rule is the capability the system must provide to meet that need, for example "The system shall display the availability status of every catalogued title to any logged-in member." It is written for developers and testers, is precise about who and what, and can be tested. The documented form is the written record of either one, such as a user story card or a numbered SRS entry. What it uniquely contributes is persistence and shared reference: a need voiced in a meeting lives only in memory and drifts, whereas the written record communicates one single interpretation to engineer, tester and client alike, preserves it across the project, and allows it to be reviewed, traced back to the stakeholder who asked for it, and traced forward to a design decision and a test case.

question_text: A team building an online examination portal has run out of time and must cut scope two weeks before release. Using the MoSCoW technique, explain the difference between a "Should have" and a "Could have" requirement, and explain why it is still worth formally recording the items the team has agreed NOT to build in this release.
rubric: 1 mark for explaining Should have (important but not vital, a workaround exists). 1 mark for explaining Could have (desirable, adds value, not critical to core function). 1 mark for articulating the boundary between the two rather than placing two definitions side by side, ideally with an exam portal example. 1 mark for one sound, developed reason for recording Won't haves.
model_answer: A Should have is important but not vital for the first release: its absence causes real pain, but the system still functions and the gap can be temporarily worked around. Automatic emailing of results is a Should have for the exam portal, since an administrator can send them manually instead. A Could have is desirable and adds value but is not critical to the core function, and nothing has to be worked around if it is absent, such as a screen showing a student's past attempts. The distinction is therefore the consequence of omission and whether someone must fill the gap by other means, so with two weeks left the team drops Could haves first. Recording the Won't haves is still worthwhile because it turns the exclusion into an agreed, written decision rather than an oversight, it prevents the item being quietly reintroduced during the final fortnight as scope creep, it manages stakeholder expectations honestly by showing that a request was heard and deferred rather than ignored, and it preserves the analysis already done as the starting point for the next release.
student_answer: Since with the time issue, team has to implement some feature more quickly by reducing certain extra functionalities and maybe remove some non mandatory functionalities.   Should have -> Implementations that needs to developed somehow with the time, since these functionalities might affect other parts of the software   Could have -> Implementations that can be cut out from the development procedure, since these might be independent and doesnt affect overall software performance.      It is still worth formally recording the items the team has agreed not to build in this release, since the clients might get a different output than they expected. With the formal recording client knows which caused these.

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Validation asks whether the requirements reflect what stakeholders actually need, which can only be answered against real people and real source documents that the tool cannot access, so an independent human review is essential. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.
student_answer: In the core AI tools uses prediction logics.   When using AI to help record requirements, hallucinations and many other issues might happen,   -> Adding new unrelated data for requirements   -> Creating a requirements that gives many meanings   -> Creating requirements that a human cant clearly understand   Using the same tool to check the quality of the requirements is useless, since its the tool that was trained by the same data set that caused these faults.      Clearly the software engineer in-charge of developing the certain part carries the professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail, since he should always understand clearly what each requirement means, by reaching out to client again and again if needed. Human should always have the complete clear idea of the system and should not be dependent on a tool completely.

question_text: A consultant skipped fact-finding entirely and began interviewing staff at a client's warehouse on day one. Describe two specific outputs that fact-finding would have produced before those interviews began, and explain how agreeing the system's scope at this early stage reduces requirement instability later in the project.
rubric: 1 mark for a first valid fact-finding output identified and given specific warehouse content (half marks if merely named with no context). 1 mark for a second, genuinely distinct output given specific content. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism, that an agreed scope acts as a baseline so later out-of-scope requests are recognised and handled as changes. 1 mark for linking this explicitly to reduced requirement instability, less rework, or less scope creep.
model_answer: The first output is a defined system scope with boundaries and external interfaces: an agreed statement that goods receipt, put-away, picking and stock levels are included, that payroll and rostering for warehouse staff are excluded, and that an interface to the existing accounting package is required. Without it every request a storeman raises sounds equally in scope. The second is an overview of the existing processes together with an identified stakeholder list across all levels, mapping how goods currently move through the warehouse and naming the floor staff, the stock controller, the dispatch supervisor, the finance team who consume the stock figures and the IT staff who will maintain the system, since otherwise the consultant cannot know whom to interview and will forget exactly those groups. Agreeing scope reduces later instability because the boundary becomes a baseline: every requirement collected afterwards can be tested against it, so a request falling outside is recognised as a change to be costed and approved rather than absorbed silently as scope creep. It also forces disagreements to surface in week one for the price of a meeting rather than in month five for the price of a redesign, and because the exclusions are explicit it removes the largest source of late argument, which is the assumption that the system would obviously cover something.

question_text: A consultant skipped fact-finding entirely and began interviewing staff at a client's warehouse on day one. Describe two specific outputs that fact-finding would have produced before those interviews began, and explain how agreeing the system's scope at this early stage reduces requirement instability later in the project.
rubric: 1 mark for a first valid fact-finding output identified and given specific warehouse content (half marks if merely named with no context). 1 mark for a second, genuinely distinct output given specific content. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism, that an agreed scope acts as a baseline so later out-of-scope requests are recognised and handled as changes. 1 mark for linking this explicitly to reduced requirement instability, less rework, or less scope creep.
model_answer: The first output is a defined system scope with boundaries and external interfaces: an agreed statement that goods receipt, put-away, picking and stock levels are included, that payroll and rostering for warehouse staff are excluded, and that an interface to the existing accounting package is required. Without it every request a storeman raises sounds equally in scope. The second is an overview of the existing processes together with an identified stakeholder list across all levels, mapping how goods currently move through the warehouse and naming the floor staff, the stock controller, the dispatch supervisor, the finance team who consume the stock figures and the IT staff who will maintain the system, since otherwise the consultant cannot know whom to interview and will forget exactly those groups. Agreeing scope reduces later instability because the boundary becomes a baseline: every requirement collected afterwards can be tested against it, so a request falling outside is recognised as a change to be costed and approved rather than absorbed silently as scope creep. It also forces disagreements to surface in week one for the price of a meeting rather than in month five for the price of a redesign, and because the exclusions are explicit it removes the largest source of late argument, which is the assumption that the system would obviously cover something.
student_answer: Fact finding helps to gather an idea about the requirements from the outside system. Then getting interviews helps the team get an idea about the outside and the inside of the system.   This improves the chance of getting every requirement right.

question_text: A team building an online examination portal has run out of time and must cut scope two weeks before release. Using the MoSCoW technique, explain the difference between a "Should have" and a "Could have" requirement, and explain why it is still worth formally recording the items the team has agreed NOT to build in this release.
rubric: 1 mark for explaining Should have (important but not vital, a workaround exists). 1 mark for explaining Could have (desirable, adds value, not critical to core function). 1 mark for articulating the boundary between the two rather than placing two definitions side by side, ideally with an exam portal example. 1 mark for one sound, developed reason for recording Won't haves.
model_answer: A Should have is important but not vital for the first release: its absence causes real pain, but the system still functions and the gap can be temporarily worked around. Automatic emailing of results is a Should have for the exam portal, since an administrator can send them manually instead. A Could have is desirable and adds value but is not critical to the core function, and nothing has to be worked around if it is absent, such as a screen showing a student's past attempts. The distinction is therefore the consequence of omission and whether someone must fill the gap by other means, so with two weeks left the team drops Could haves first. Recording the Won't haves is still worthwhile because it turns the exclusion into an agreed, written decision rather than an oversight, it prevents the item being quietly reintroduced during the final fortnight as scope creep, it manages stakeholder expectations honestly by showing that a request was heard and deferred rather than ignored, and it preserves the analysis already done as the starting point for the next release.

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Validation asks whether the requirements reflect what stakeholders actually need, which can only be answered against real people and real source documents that the tool cannot access, so an independent human review is essential. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.

rubric: 1 mark for correctly characterising the user need as the goal in the user's own language. 1 mark for correctly characterising the system rule as the capability the system must provide to meet it. 1 mark for a valid self-chosen example carried consistently through both forms. 1 mark for identifying a distinct contribution of the documented form (durable record, single shared interpretation, traceability, or something to validate against).
model_answer: A user need is the goal expressed in the user's own language, for example "I want to know whether a book is on the shelf before I walk across campus to fetch it." It states what the person is trying to achieve and says nothing about the system. A system rule is the capability the system must provide to meet that need, for example "The system shall display the availability status of every catalogued title to any logged-in member." It is written for developers and testers, is precise about who and what, and can be tested. The documented form is the written record of either one, such as a user story card or a numbered SRS entry. What it uniquely contributes is persistence and shared reference: a need voiced in a meeting lives only in memory and drifts, whereas the written record communicates one single interpretation to engineer, tester and client alike, preserves it across the project, and allows it to be reviewed, traced back to the stakeholder who asked for it, and traced forward to a design decision and a test case.

question_text: A team building an online examination portal has run out of time and must cut scope two weeks before release. Using the MoSCoW technique, explain the difference between a "Should have" and a "Could have" requirement, and explain why it is still worth formally recording the items the team has agreed NOT to build in this release.
rubric: 1 mark for explaining Should have (important but not vital, a workaround exists). 1 mark for explaining Could have (desirable, adds value, not critical to core function). 1 mark for articulating the boundary between the two rather than placing two definitions side by side, ideally with an exam portal example. 1 mark for one sound, developed reason for recording Won't haves.
model_answer: A Should have is important but not vital for the first release: its absence causes real pain, but the system still functions and the gap can be temporarily worked around. Automatic emailing of results is a Should have for the exam portal, since an administrator can send them manually instead. A Could have is desirable and adds value but is not critical to the core function, and nothing has to be worked around if it is absent, such as a screen showing a student's past attempts. The distinction is therefore the consequence of omission and whether someone must fill the gap by other means, so with two weeks left the team drops Could haves first. Recording the Won't haves is still worthwhile because it turns the exclusion into an agreed, written decision rather than an oversight, it prevents the item being quietly reintroduced during the final fortnight as scope creep, it manages stakeholder expectations honestly by showing that a request was heard and deferred rather than ignored, and it preserves the analysis already done as the starting point for the next release.

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Validation asks whether the requirements reflect what stakeholders actually need, which can only be answered against real people and real source documents that the tool cannot access, so an independent human review is essential. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.

question_text: A consultant skipped fact-finding entirely and began interviewing staff at a client's warehouse on day one. Describe two specific outputs that fact-finding would have produced before those interviews began, and explain how agreeing the system's scope at this early stage reduces requirement instability later in the project.
rubric: 1 mark for a first valid fact-finding output identified and given specific warehouse content (half marks if merely named with no context). 1 mark for a second, genuinely distinct output given specific content. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism, that an agreed scope acts as a baseline so later out-of-scope requests are recognised and handled as changes. 1 mark for linking this explicitly to reduced requirement instability, less rework, or less scope creep.
model_answer: The first output is a defined system scope with boundaries and external interfaces: an agreed statement that goods receipt, put-away, picking and stock levels are included, that payroll and rostering for warehouse staff are excluded, and that an interface to the existing accounting package is required. Without it every request a storeman raises sounds equally in scope. The second is an overview of the existing processes together with an identified stakeholder list across all levels, mapping how goods currently move through the warehouse and naming the floor staff, the stock controller, the dispatch supervisor, the finance team who consume the stock figures and the IT staff who will maintain the system, since otherwise the consultant cannot know whom to interview and will forget exactly those groups. Agreeing scope reduces later instability because the boundary becomes a baseline: every requirement collected afterwards can be tested against it, so a request falling outside is recognised as a change to be costed and approved rather than absorbed silently as scope creep. It also forces disagreements to surface in week one for the price of a meeting rather than in month five for the price of a redesign, and because the exclusions are explicit it removes the largest source of late argument, which is the assumption that the system would obviously cover something.

question_text: A requirement can appear in three different forms during a project: as a user need, as a system rule, and as a documented form. Using an example of your own choosing, explain the difference between a user need and a system rule, and then state what the documented form contributes that the other two, on their own, cannot.
rubric: 1 mark for correctly characterising the user need as the goal in the user's own language. 1 mark for correctly characterising the system rule as the capability the system must provide to meet it. 1 mark for a valid self-chosen example carried consistently through both forms. 1 mark for identifying a distinct contribution of the documented form (durable record, single shared interpretation, traceability, or something to validate against).
model_answer: A user need is the goal expressed in the user's own language, for example "I want to know whether a book is on the shelf before I walk across campus to fetch it." It states what the person is trying to achieve and says nothing about the system. A system rule is the capability the system must provide to meet that need, for example "The system shall display the availability status of every catalogued title to any logged-in member." It is written for developers and testers, is precise about who and what, and can be tested. The documented form is the written record of either one, such as a user story card or a numbered SRS entry. What it uniquely contributes is persistence and shared reference: a need voiced in a meeting lives only in memory and drifts, whereas the written record communicates one single interpretation to engineer, tester and client alike, preserves it across the project, and allows it to be reviewed, traced back to the stakeholder who asked for it, and traced forward to a design decision and a test case.

question_text: A team building an online examination portal has run out of time and must cut scope two weeks before release. Using the MoSCoW technique, explain the difference between a "Should have" and a "Could have" requirement, and explain why it is still worth formally recording the items the team has agreed NOT to build in this release.
rubric: 1 mark for explaining Should have (important but not vital, a workaround exists). 1 mark for explaining Could have (desirable, adds value, not critical to core function). 1 mark for articulating the boundary between the two rather than placing two definitions side by side, ideally with an exam portal example. 1 mark for one sound, developed reason for recording Won't haves.
model_answer: A Should have is important but not vital for the first release: its absence causes real pain, but the system still functions and the gap can be temporarily worked around. Automatic emailing of results is a Should have for the exam portal, since an administrator can send them manually instead. A Could have is desirable and adds value but is not critical to the core function, and nothing has to be worked around if it is absent, such as a screen showing a student's past attempts. The distinction is therefore the consequence of omission and whether someone must fill the gap by other means, so with two weeks left the team drops Could haves first. Recording the Won't haves is still worthwhile because it turns the exclusion into an agreed, written decision rather than an oversight, it prevents the item being quietly reintroduced during the final fortnight as scope creep, it manages stakeholder expectations honestly by showing that a request was heard and deferred rather than ignored, and it preserves the analysis already done as the starting point for the next release.

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Validation asks whether the requirements reflect what stakeholders actually need, which can only be answered against real people and real source documents that the tool cannot access, so an independent human review is essential. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.

System Rule:      Definition: Represents the constraints, logic, or automated behaviors that the software system must enforce to operate correctly and securely. Example: The system must automatically generate a "Quick Reorder" list based on the users purchase history from the last 30 days, excluding any items that are currently out of stock. On their own, a spoken user need and an unwritten system rule are prone to misinterpretation, memory loss, and misalignment.
