rubric: 1 mark for a first valid fact-finding output identified and given specific warehouse content (half marks if merely named with no context). 1 mark for a second, genuinely distinct output given specific content. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism, that an agreed scope acts as a baseline so later out-of-scope requests are recognised and handled as changes. 1 mark for linking this explicitly to reduced requirement instability, less rework, or less scope creep.
model_answer: The first output is a defined system scope with boundaries and external interfaces: an agreed statement that goods receipt, put-away, picking and stock levels are included, that payroll and rostering for warehouse staff are excluded, and that an interface to the existing accounting package is required. Without it every request a storeman raises sounds equally in scope. The second is an overview of the existing processes together with an identified stakeholder list across all levels, mapping how goods currently move through the warehouse and naming the floor staff, the stock controller, the dispatch supervisor, the finance team who consume the stock figures and the IT staff who will maintain the system, since otherwise the consultant cannot know whom to interview and will forget exactly those groups. Agreeing scope reduces later instability because the boundary becomes a baseline: every requirement collected afterwards can be tested against it, so a request falling outside is recognised as a change to be costed and approved rather than absorbed silently as scope creep. It also forces disagreements to surface in week one for the price of a meeting rather than in month five for the price of a redesign, and because the exclusions are explicit it removes the largest source of late argument, which is the assumption that the system would obviously cover something.
student_answer: 1.Stakeholder list :Identifies who should be interviewed and their roles.   2.Current system/process information : Documents how the warehouse operates and existing problems.   Defining scope early prevents unnecessary changes, reduces misunderstanding, and makes requirements more stable throughout the project

question_text: A requirement can appear in three different forms during a project: as a user need, as a system rule, and as a documented form. Using an example of your own choosing, explain the difference between a user need and a system rule, and then state what the documented form contributes that the other two, on their own, cannot.
rubric: 1 mark for correctly characterising the user need as the goal in the user's own language. 1 mark for correctly characterising the system rule as the capability the system must provide to meet it. 1 mark for a valid self-chosen example carried consistently through both forms. 1 mark for identifying a distinct contribution of the documented form (durable record, single shared interpretation, traceability, or something to validate against).
model_answer: A user need is the goal expressed in the user's own language, for example "I want to know whether a book is on the shelf before I walk across campus to fetch it." It states what the person is trying to achieve and says nothing about the system. A system rule is the capability the system must provide to meet that need, for example "The system shall display the availability status of every catalogued title to any logged-in member." It is written for developers and testers, is precise about who and what, and can be tested. The documented form is the written record of either one, such as a user story card or a numbered SRS entry. What it uniquely contributes is persistence and shared reference: a need voiced in a meeting lives only in memory and drifts, whereas the written record communicates one single interpretation to engineer, tester and client alike, preserves it across the project, and allows it to be reviewed, traced back to the stakeholder who asked for it, and traced forward to a design decision and a test case.
student_answer: A user may want to record and later retrieve his daily goals in an app.

question_text: A team building an online examination portal has run out of time and must cut scope two weeks before release. Using the MoSCoW technique, explain the difference between a "Should have" and a "Could have" requirement, and explain why it is still worth formally recording the items the team has agreed NOT to build in this release.
rubric: 1 mark for explaining Should have (important but not vital, a workaround exists). 1 mark for explaining Could have (desirable, adds value, not critical to core function). 1 mark for articulating the boundary between the two rather than placing two definitions side by side, ideally with an exam portal example. 1 mark for one sound, developed reason for recording Won't haves.
model_answer: A Should have is important but not vital for the first release: its absence causes real pain, but the system still functions and the gap can be temporarily worked around. Automatic emailing of results is a Should have for the exam portal, since an administrator can send them manually instead. A Could have is desirable and adds value but is not critical to the core function, and nothing has to be worked around if it is absent, such as a screen showing a student's past attempts. The distinction is therefore the consequence of omission and whether someone must fill the gap by other means, so with two weeks left the team drops Could haves first. Recording the Won't haves is still worthwhile because it turns the exclusion into an agreed, written decision rather than an oversight, it prevents the item being quietly reintroduced during the final fortnight as scope creep, it manages stakeholder expectations honestly by showing that a request was heard and deferred rather than ignored, and it preserves the analysis already done as the starting point for the next release.

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Validation asks whether the requirements reflect what stakeholders actually need, which can only be answered against real people and real source documents that the tool cannot access, so an independent human review is essential. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.
student_answer: Because ai models are tools that are created with a given set of parameters and and when we are checking the quality of the requirements it has produced using the same tool it only looks for those same factors unless we specifically tells it to. This can cause potential bugs in the system and most probably the developer or the  company will have to bear the consequences of the system failures.

rubric: 1 mark for explaining Should have (important but not vital, a workaround exists). 1 mark for explaining Could have (desirable, adds value, not critical to core function). 1 mark for articulating the boundary between the two rather than placing two definitions side by side, ideally with an exam portal example. 1 mark for one sound, developed reason for recording Won't haves.
model_answer: A Should have is important but not vital for the first release: its absence causes real pain, but the system still functions and the gap can be temporarily worked around. Automatic emailing of results is a Should have for the exam portal, since an administrator can send them manually instead. A Could have is desirable and adds value but is not critical to the core function, and nothing has to be worked around if it is absent, such as a screen showing a student's past attempts. The distinction is therefore the consequence of omission and whether someone must fill the gap by other means, so with two weeks left the team drops Could haves first. Recording the Won't haves is still worthwhile because it turns the exclusion into an agreed, written decision rather than an oversight, it prevents the item being quietly reintroduced during the final fortnight as scope creep, it manages stakeholder expectations honestly by showing that a request was heard and deferred rather than ignored, and it preserves the analysis already done as the starting point for the next release.

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the circularity or self-confirmation problem. 1 mark for a concrete consequence (undetected ambiguity, invented requirements passing as well formed, or false confidence produced by fluent output). 1 mark for identifying the remedy or the reason it is needed (independent human review; validation must be against real stakeholders and real source documents). 1 mark for stating unambiguously that the human engineer who accepted the requirement is accountable and that responsibility does not transfer to the tool.
model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. Ambiguity it failed to notice while writing it will fail to notice while reviewing, because the interpretation it holds is the one it wrote from. This matters most for the two failure modes AI is prone to. A model can invent requirements that no stakeholder ever expressed, and asked to check such a statement it will find it well formed, because well formedness is a property of the wording rather than of whether a real person asked for it. Because fluent output reads as authoritative, a requirement returned as "checked" attracts less scrutiny than a colleague's draft would. Validation asks whether the requirements reflect what stakeholders actually need, which can only be answered against real people and real source documents that the tool cannot access, so an independent human review is essential. Professional responsibility rests with the engineer who accepted the requirement and put their name to the specification; accountability does not transfer to the tool or its vendor.

question_text: A consultant skipped fact-finding entirely and began interviewing staff at a client's warehouse on day one. Describe two specific outputs that fact-finding would have produced before those interviews began, and explain how agreeing the system's scope at this early stage reduces requirement instability later in the project.
rubric: 1 mark for a first valid fact-finding output identified and given specific warehouse content (half marks if merely named with no context). 1 mark for a second, genuinely distinct output given specific content. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism, that an agreed scope acts as a baseline so later out-of-scope requests are recognised and handled as changes. 1 mark for linking this explicitly to reduced requirement instability, less rework, or less scope creep.
model_answer: The first output is a defined system scope with boundaries and external interfaces: an agreed statement that goods receipt, put-away, picking and stock levels are included, that payroll and rostering for warehouse staff are excluded, and that an interface to the existing accounting package is required. Without it every request a storeman raises sounds equally in scope. The second is an overview of the existing processes together with an identified stakeholder list across all levels, mapping how goods currently move through the warehouse and naming the floor staff, the stock controller, the dispatch supervisor, the finance team who consume the stock figures and the IT staff who will maintain the system, since otherwise the consultant cannot know whom to interview and will forget exactly those groups. Agreeing scope reduces later instability because the boundary becomes a baseline: every requirement collected afterwards can be tested against it, so a request falling outside is recognised as a change to be costed and approved rather than absorbed silently as scope creep. It also forces disagreements to surface in week one for the price of a meeting rather than in month five for the price of a redesign, and because the exclusions are explicit it removes the largest source of late argument, which is the assumption that the system would obviously cover something.

question_text: A requirement can appear in three different forms during a project: as a user need, as a system rule, and as a documented form. Using an example of your own choosing, explain the difference between a user need and a system rule, and then state what the documented form contributes that the other two, on their own, cannot.
rubric: 1 mark for correctly characterising the user need as the goal in the user's own language. 1 mark for correctly characterising the system rule as the capability the system must provide to meet it. 1 mark for a valid self-chosen example carried consistently through both forms. 1 mark for identifying a distinct contribution of the documented form (durable record, single shared interpretation, traceability, or something to validate against).
model_answer: A user need is the goal expressed in the user's own language, for example "I want to know whether a book is on the shelf before I walk across campus to fetch it." It states what the person is trying to achieve and says nothing about the system. A system rule is the capability the system must provide to meet that need, for example "The system shall display the availability status of every catalogued title to any logged-in member." It is written for developers and testers, is precise about who and what, and can be tested. The documented form is the written record of either one, such as a user story card or a numbered SRS entry. What it uniquely contributes is persistence and shared reference: a need voiced in a meeting lives only in memory and drifts, whereas the written record communicates one single interpretation to engineer, tester and client alike, preserves it across the project, and allows it to be reviewed, traced back to the stakeholder who asked for it, and traced forward to a design decision and a test case.

question_text: AI tools are increasingly used in requirements work to draft user stories and to reword unclear requirements. Explain the danger of allowing the same tool to then check the quality of the requirements it has just produced, and state clearly who carries professional responsibility if one of those requirements later causes the delivered system to fail.

model_answer: The danger is circularity: a tool that checks its own output applies the same assumptions, vocabulary and blind spots to the review that it used in the draft, so it confirms itself rather than testing anything. question_text: A consultant skipped fact-finding entirely and began interviewing staff at a client's warehouse on day one. Describe two specific outputs that fact-finding would have produced before those interviews began, and explain how agreeing the system's scope at this early stage reduces requirement instability later in the project.
rubric: 1 mark for a first valid fact-finding output identified and given specific warehouse content (half marks if merely named with no context). 1 mark for a second, genuinely distinct output given specific content. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism, that an agreed scope acts as a baseline so later out-of-scope requests are recognised and handled as changes. 1 mark for linking this explicitly to reduced requirement instability, less rework, or less scope creep.
model_answer: The first output is a defined system scope with boundaries and external interfaces: an agreed statement that goods receipt, put-away, picking and stock levels are included, that payroll and rostering for warehouse staff are excluded, and that an interface to the existing accounting package is required. Without it every request a storeman raises sounds equally in scope. The second is an overview of the existing processes together with an identified stakeholder list across all levels, mapping how goods currently move through the warehouse and naming the floor staff, the stock controller, the dispatch supervisor, the finance team who consume the stock figures and the IT staff who will maintain the system, since otherwise the consultant cannot know whom to interview and will forget exactly those groups. Agreeing scope reduces later instability because the boundary becomes a baseline: every requirement collected afterwards can be tested against it, so a request falling outside is recognised as a change to be costed and approved rather than absorbed silently as scope creep. It also forces disagreements to surface in week one for the price of a meeting rather than in month five for the price of a redesign, and because the exclusions are explicit it removes the largest source of late argument, which is the assumption that the system would obviously cover something.
